summary_sentence: Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical 'Magnifica Humanitas' called for AI to be 'disarmed' with Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah on the Vatican stage; major outlets (TechCrunch, Bloomberg, FT, The Information, The Register, The Verge, Variety) framed it as a power-concentration critique while a CNN TT clip pushed the 'disarmed' soundbite to 578k engagement.
praises: iScienceLuvr cites the encyclical's nuanced framing that technology takes on the characteristics of those who devise and fund it, not inherently evil
Chris Olah's invitation to present alongside the Pope frames Anthropic as the lab the Vatican wanted in the room
complaints: Pope Leo's framing positions current AI development as risking 'New Forms of Dehumanization' under opaque control of few firms
TechCrunch argues the encyclical 'isn't really about AI' but uses AI as a lens for older concerns about concentrated power
FT highlights the 'idolatry of profit' framing critiquing the entire commercial AI revolution

creator_recommendation.angle: Read the actual encyclical (it's online) and unpack the three technical claims it makes about modern AI from a builder's perspective; map each claim to the actual mechanism it describes (training data ownership, model concentration, agent autonomy) rather than the theological framing.
creator_recommendation.hook: The Pope's first encyclical names three things wrong with AI. Two of them are real engineering decisions you make every week. Here is what he actually said, and what to change in your stack.
